4753.dq: aucune ne présente actuellement de phénomène d'accent, d'intensité ni de longueur. (The denial is not restricted to any level: no accent, intensity or length phenomenon at all, so word-level stress is denied a fortiori; the surrounding discussion concerns tone modification at word junctures within the phrase.)
4753.dloc: p. 285, chapter 'Récapitulation contrastive', Remarque 2 (directly below the table of tonal-modification subareas whose rows a3 = 'kara, lai, toongo' and a4 = "'buli, 'biy., mbo."); cross-reference p. 345 ('Correspondances phoniques'), Remarque. Read on from the Google Books publisher preview; informant identity pp. 51-52.
4753.prule: No stress. The source states that none of the Gbaya languages concerned (the tonal-modification area a, whose table rows explicitly list toongo (a3) and 'buli, 'biyanda (a4), i.e. the Southwest Gbaya varieties) shows any phenomenon of accent, intensity or length; they are tone languages in which low tone schemes are raised before a term with a high first tonal mora depending on syllable structure (the 'marqueur de relation' tone sandhi). A word accent is entertained only as a hypothesis for a stage earlier than proto-Gbaya (p. 345).
4753.quote: [p. 285] Remarque 2. A la question, soulevée par Jacqueline THOMAS, de savoir si les différences de traitement tonal en fonction du type syllabique ne pourraient s'expliquer par la présence d'un accent dans les langues concernées, on doit répondre négativement: aucune ne présente actuellement de phénomène d'accent, d'intensité ni de longueur. L'hypothèse sera reposée en diachronie, lors de l'interprétation des correspondances phoniques (p. 345). [p. 345] Remarque. 4753.exq_: L'absence d'accent dans les langues actuelles n'impose pas cette solution en proto-gbaya, mais l'hypothèse est envisageable à un niveau antérieur de l'évolution. (No exceptions to the no-accent statement; only a diachronic hypothesis of a pre-proto-Gbaya accent.)
4753.tone: Tone language: the p. 285 table works with 'schèmes bas' (low tone schemes, marked CV̀, CV̀C, CV̀V̀, CV̀CV̀, CV̀CV̀CV̀) that become high or rising before a following term whose first tonal mora is high, conditioned by syllable structure; toongo is in subarea a3 (low becomes high on CV̀, rising on CV̀C, CV̀V̀, CV̀CV̀, CV̀CV̀CV̀), 'buli and 'biyanda in a4 (low becomes rising on every syllable type, never plain high). This tonal-modification 'marqueur de relation' is described as morphological/syntactic tone sandhi ('modification tonale morphologique'), not accent; the source explicitly denies accent, intensity and length as explanations. The number of tone levels for the gso varieties is not on the held pages (the Northwest sister has two levels, four tones per Roulon-Doko & Dui 2024, p. 2).

4754.dq: The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word. [examples (5): aca 'yat 'I have taken it'; 'mony dit 'old man'; 'yok luac 'pregnant cows'; 'lec 'teeth']
4754.dloc: Malou 1988 ch. 2 'An overview of Dinka phonological structure', sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word' p. 9 and examples (5) p. 10.
4754.prule: No stress-placement rule is stated. Malou (pan-Dinka): every syllable carries one tone; each pause-bounded 'phonological word' carries exactly one non-contrastive stress whose conditioning 'has not been studied'. His marked examples (5) put the stress on the lexical head/root of the unit (aca 'yat 'I have taken it', 'muoc met 'give the child something', 'mony dit 'old man', 'yok luac 'pregnant cows', 'lec 'teeth'), but he draws no rule from them. SW-specific description (Remijsen & Manyang 2009, Luanyjang = Rek cluster): four tonemes (Low, High, Rise, Fall), one per morpheme, associated with the rightmost (usually only) syllable; predictable non-distinctive high pitch on the penult of polysyllables; no word stress described.
4754.srule: None within the phonological word: 'Each phonological word has one and only one stress... one syllable is stressed in each word' (Malou 1988: 9; his phonological word is pause-bounded and may span two lexical words, e.g. 'mony dit 'old man'). No secondary or rhythmic stress is described in any source opened (Malou 1988 ch. 2; Gilley 2004; Remijsen & Ladd 2008; Remijsen & Manyang 2009; Blum 2023).

4754.tone: Malou 1988 sec. 2.3: 'the syllable in Dinka is the unit of tone placement. Every syllable carries one and only one tone.' Remijsen & Manyang 2009 p. 120: 'There are four distinctive tone patterns (tonemes) - Low, High, Rise, and Fall. Each morpheme carries one, irrespective of its number of syllables. This toneme associates with the rightmost syllable, which is usually the only syllable. In polysyllabic words, the penultimate syllable may have high pitch. This high pitch is not distinctive. Rather, it is predictable given the toneme on the final syllable.' Stress in the SW-specific sources appears only in the Gilley footnote and in reference titles; Nebel 1948 (Rek-Malual) uses 'accent(uated)' only for grammatical prominence (positive vs negative verb grade, case lengthening), never for a word-stress position.

4764.prule: Stress is lexically specified within the last two syllables. Davis's convention is that stress is penultimate unless the entry is annotated 'final', and 126 of the 341 entries (37 percent) carry that annotation, on underived roots of every shape (elima 'hand', dalan 'road', likod 'back', mata 'eye', bulan 'moon', dua 'two', lima 'five', ako 'I') and on affixed forms (kumaan/mengaan 'eat', lumuak/mengluak 'plant', lumipak/meglipak 'hit', meneginep 'dream'). No phonological conditioning is stated, and a check of the saved list finds none: final stress occurs both in vowel-final words (12 of 52) and consonant/glottal-final words (112 of 273), and with every penult vowel (a 23/107, e 28/73, i 36/79, u 36/62), so no category is categorically penult or final; there is only a gradient tendency for final stress to be commoner after high penult vowels. Thiessen (1981:10, via Zorc) independently confines word accent in Canipaan and three sister varieties to 'one of the last two syllables of a word' and calls it non-contrastive; Davis's item-by-item marking shows that the choice within that window is a property of the individual word.

4770.prule: Fused tone-accent ('tono-acento') system: each word has exactly one accented syllable, and that syllable carries one of three contrastive tone-accent phonemes (high, low, falling), lexically distinctive (minimal pairs kudû 'diablo' / kudù 'piedra', tikí? 'flecha' / tikî? 'hule') with no grammatical function; all other syllables carry non-contrastive, mechanically produced secondary tones; accented vowels are slightly lengthened. 4770.tone: Manrique frames the system as three suprasegmental 'tono-acento' phonemes (alto, bajo, descendente), one and only one per word, phonemic by minimal pairs but without grammatical function (unlike other Pamean languages); unaccented syllables have mechanical secondary tones; accented vowels lengthen slightly (p. 13); phrase melody rises slowly and falls abruptly at the end with no declarative/interrogative difference (p. 17). The 1967 English version calls them 'tone-stress phonemes' (Google Books, p. 334). Berthiaume (2012: 9) reads the Pame descriptions as 'fundamentally a pitch-accent system' and infers, explicitly as his own inference, that stress falls on the lexical root. A pitch-accent reading is thus defensible; either way the source gives no placement rule, hence tone or pitch accent.

Monosyllabic words and clitics are stressed.

4772.tone: Plainly tonal: 'Modern Ixtlan has four different tones on accented final syllables: low, high, rising, falling. On accented penults, there are only three: low, high, falling.' Tone is licensed by the accent: it affects 'the accented syllable and the one following it, if there is one', with five attested two-syllable patterns (low-low, high-low, falling-low, high-high, low-high); rising and falling never occur before glottal stop. 4776.dloc: Lautlehre, 'Accent und Quantität', §§28-33, pp. 43-47; the quoted §§29-31 are on pp. 44-45
4776.heavy: 'lang' = a syllable with a long vowel, as marked in Patkanov's and Castrén's transcriptions (§33: syllable quantity 'kann nicht durch allgemeine Regeln angegeben werden' and is often hard to determine); the verbal suffixes -χamd, -χumd, -χind, -χend, -kend, -as, -id, -umd, -ant, -ad count as long, -es, -eŋed, -em, -ed as short (§29); a closed final syllable with a short vowel counts as short (§30: consonant-final nouns 'wenn dieselbe kurz ist').
4776.dflt: antepenult in words of three or more syllables (§31: 'nur in mehrsilbigen Wörtern, deren zwei letzten Silben kurz sind', e.g. tévedem, tabetmet, veresem); penult in disyllables (§29a p. 44: 'Selbstverständlich ist der Accent energischer, wenn die vorletzte Silbe lang und die letzte kurz ist, als wenn beide kurz sind'); in all-short words the stressed syllable is 'kaum vor den anderen hervorgehoben' (§28)
4776.prule: Word stress lies within a three-syllable window at the right edge and is decided by vowel length: penult by default (the majority of base forms); final in disyllables whose final syllable is long and first syllable short (and optionally in consonant-final nouns, loanwords and adverbs even with a short final); antepenult only in words of three or more syllables whose last two syllables are short; in polysyllables the penult is stressed only if it is long (a listed set of long verbal suffixes counts as long).
4776.srule: Not mentioned in Patkanov & Fuchs 1906, 'Accent und Quantität' §§ 28-33, pp. 43-47 (read in full): no word-internal secondary or rhythmic stress is described; the only weaker accents mentioned are on whole words in phrases (postpositions 'immer schwach betont') and enclitics without 'selbständigen Accent'.

4777.dq: For the pronunciation of words a general rule can be made that the accent falls on the penultimate, as in Malay, Dayak, Javanese, Sundanese, &c. [Beech p. 19] ... Suffixes may cause a shift of accent to the new penult, the suffix being felt as part of the word to which it has been added [Fokker p. 109]
4777.dloc: Beech, 'Alphabet and pronunciation', p. 19; Fokker, Appendix § 8, p. 109
4777.heavy: The only condition stated is vowel quality: a penult that 'does not contain ĕ (medio-palatal, French e muet)' takes the accent; a penult containing ĕ (schwa) does not, the accent then falling on the final syllable by the examples (tĕráŋ, kĕpá', gĕnáp). No vowel-length or coda condition is stated; kasábay, bálay, dinándu (closed finals, penult accent) show that a closed final does not attract the accent.
4777.dflt: final syllable when the penult contains ĕ (given by example only, all disyllables, and all three accented examples are Bolongan forms; the sole Tarakan example mĕñjul carries no accent mark; the case of ĕ in both penult and final is not addressed)
4777.prule: Accent on the penultimate syllable of the word, provided the penult does not contain ĕ (schwa, 'medio-palatal, French e muet'); when the penult has ĕ the accent lies on the final syllable (shown by example only: Bolongan tĕráŋ, kĕpá', gĕnáp; the one Tarakan example mĕñjul is printed without an accent mark). Schwa penults are 'extremely rare' in Tarakan (= Southern Tidung proper), so the language is penult-accented in practice. Suffixes on vowel-final stems count as part of the word and shift the accent to the new penult (nusáï, naŋkúbi, sāmá-mu); the enclitic particles nia (Tar.) / na (Bol.) 'already' are not suffixes and leave the original accent in place (pupus-nia). The p. 58 footnote (pa-báïs 'to adjust', 'the accent falls on the second syllable') is consistent with the penult rule (pa-bá-ïs), not an exception.
4777.srule: Not mentioned in Beech 1908 (Fokker's Appendix § 7-8 'Accent', pp. 109-110, and Beech 'Alphabet and pronunciation' p. 19, read in full): a single word accent is described and its shift under suffixation; no secondary or rhythmic accent is discussed.

4779.dq: First, accent placement is lexically specified and the relevant domain is the word rather than the syllable. Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents.
4779.dloc: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe', pp. 15-16; sec. 4.2.1, p. 24; sec. 4.2.3, pp. 25-26; sec. 5.4, p. 53.
4779.prule: One obligatory, culminative accent per phonological word (exponents: high F0, duration, amplitude; unaccented vowels gradiently devoiced or deleted). Its position is lexically specified: simplex disyllables are either trochees /*Ø-Ø/ (high-initial) or iambs /Ø-*Ø/ (high-final, the most common disyllabic pattern), plus a third class /*L-Ø/ where a privative /L/ tone on the accented syllable is realised as a rise. No positional or weight-based rule; frequency count shows trochees and iambs 'equally distributed' with a slight iambic tendency.
4779.srule: None: accent is 'culminative (“at most one per word”)' at the level of the phonological word; no secondary or rhythmic stresses described (Sims 2017, secs. 3.7, 4-5 read; six-syllable prosodic words carry one accent mark, p. 15). Two-accent compounds are analysed as two phonological words (p. 39 fn. 20).
4779.quote: In Yonghe, accent is obligatory, culminative, and lexically specified. [...] I use the term 'accent' as opposed to 'stress' for three different reasons. First, accent placement is lexically specified and the relevant domain is the word rather than the syllable. Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents. Third, 'stress' generally refers to relative prominence, however, as will be discussed below, Yonghe accent is not strictly an issue of relative prominence…
4779.loc: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe', pp. 15-16; sec. 4.2.1, p. 24; sec. 4.2.3, pp. 25-26; sec. 5.4, p. 53.

4779.tone: Sims 2017 analyses Yonghe as having stress-accent plus a privative /L/ tone contrast (p. 52: 'Yonghe is unique among Rma/Qiang varieties in possessing contrastive tone in addition to stress-accent'); accented toneless syllables are high, accented /L/ syllables rising, unaccented syllables low. Sims 2021 (PhD, ch. 3, p. 137) reframes the same data as 'Like most Tibeto-Burman languages, Yonghe Qiang is tonal' and describes pitch patterns: high-initial 'The accent pattern for these forms is trochaic' (p. 148); high-final 'it is difficult to say which syllable is more prominent. The first syllable is much longer than the second syllable, yet it has a lower pitch and intensity' (p. 151); rising-final (morphologically complex only) 'The accent pattern for these forms is iambic' (p. 156). Sims 2021 p. 18 says the 2017 thesis 'has issues with respect to the analysis of the tonal and accentual system'. Sims 2016 (L&L 17(3), pp. 353, 357) predates both: 'Suprasegmentals in Yonghe are not yet well understood'; 'It is not clear whether or not Yonghe has lexical tones... syllable pitch... is predictable from the stress patterns of polysyllabic words'. So the accent-vs-tone framing is unsettled between the author's own works, but no source gives a positional stress rule; the lexical accent is the constant across them.

4780.tone: Sharma 1979 describes a three-term lexical tone system assigned per word (Tone 1 falling-rising /\/, Tone 2 level-rising /-/ unmarked, Tone 3 rising-falling /'/; pp. 104-106), with the falling-tone syllable longer than the others (p. 105), plus utterance-level intonational pitch levels (low/mid/high) and terminal contours (pp. 107-109). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the 28 scanned pages (a full-text search over the scan: no hits for stress/accent/prominen/loud/intensity); 'emphasis' appears once (p. 105) only as an environmental feature held constant when establishing tonal contrasts. Other saved sources agree the word-level contrast is tonal: LSI Himachal Pradesh 2023 Bhotia chapter (three tones + nasalization), Hein 2017 (register tone in Tabo), Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 (two-way high/low pitch tone for the W section incl. Spiti; 'The distinction of stress is attested mainly in Balti', p. 241), Mehta 2021 (three tones per Sharma; five tone-bearing words in her Pin-valley data).

4781.tone: Lexical tone is asserted first-hand: 'distinctive lexical tone' (Ivani & Zakharko 2024: 323), 'three lexical tones' (Ivani 2022: 69), and the authors say the tone description is in progress so tone is unmarked in examples (2024: 325 fn. 7). Joessing 2025 (instrumental BA study, sec. 5.3) hears a two-way contour contrast carried by the major syllable ('tone is assumed to be carried exclusively by the major syllable'). Stress: no rule, only wordhood diagnostics (primary stress per lexical unit; stress domain = whole verb complex) and the second-hand statement that minor syllables 'lack stress and tone contrasts' (Joessing 2025: 4 citing Ivani 2023).

tn.quote: Auditory assessment of the data suggested a contrast between two distinct pitch contours. Based on the established sesquisyllabic structure, tone is assumed to be carried exclusively by the major syllable ... Tone 1 remains relatively level or shows a slight terminal rise, while Tone 2 continues to fall throughout. A third tonal category was initially considered but discarded due to insufficient token count and acoustic similarity to Tone 2. ... Tonal contours are represented with diacritics: /á/ for Tone 1 (level/rising) and /à/ for Tone 2 (falling).

tn.note: Lexical tone is certain (minimal pairs, Ivani 2023/2024) but the inventory is preliminary: a BA acoustic study hears two contours on the major syllable; Ivani 2022 reports three lexical tones. Stress is the wordhood criterion (one primary stress per phonological word; the verb complex is one such word); its position is not stated.
